spray-foam-roofing.body_html:
Spray Foam Roofing Built for Clovis Heat, Fog, and Growth

Spray foam roofing in Clovis solves the two problems that kill flat roofs in the eastern Fresno County basin: seams and heat. Every conventional low-slope system — built-up gravel, modified bitumen, TPO, PVC — is assembled from pieces, and every piece has an edge. Those edges are where thermal movement concentrates, and Clovis delivers extraordinary thermal movement: rooftop surface temperatures north of 160°F on a July afternoon along Shaw Avenue, followed by a 40-degree overnight drop, repeated a hundred times a summer. Then winter arrives and tule fog keeps the same roof damp for days at a time, working moisture into every fastener hole and lap seam that summer opened up. Spray polyurethane foam sidesteps the whole failure sequence because it has no seams to open. The foam is applied as a liquid that expands and bonds monolithically to the substrate, flowing around penetrations, up parapet walls, and over curbs as a single continuous membrane. There is no edge for the heat to work on and no lap for the fog to soak.

Allstate Spray Foam Roofing has installed SPF across the Central Valley for more than twenty years. We are family-owned, fully licensed (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited, and members of the Spray Polyurethane Foam Alliance. Our crews dispatch from our Tulare County shop and reach Clovis in roughly 55 minutes via Highway 99 and CA-168 — close enough for reliable scheduling, seasoned enough that a foam rig on your roof is running its thousandth job, not its tenth.

The low-slope inventory this page is written for is broader than most owners realize. If your building has a roof you cannot see from the street — a dead-flat deck behind a parapet, a barely-pitched membrane over a strip center, a standing-seam metal roof on a shop or warehouse, a gravel built-up roof that predates the freeway — spray foam roofing is a candidate system for it. That includes multi-tenant retail where one roof spans six businesses, single-owner industrial buildings, medical and professional offices, church halls and gymnasiums, mini-storage rows, and the flat-roofed mid-century commercial stock that lines the older arterials. It also includes buildings whose existing roof is already a patchwork: because foam is applied as a liquid over a prepared surface, it bridges transitions between old repairs, mismatched membranes, and odd additions in a way no rolled or sheet product can. The assessment is where we confirm the fit — and where, occasionally, we rule it out, because a deck holding trapped moisture has to be opened and dried before anyone should spray a permanent roof over it.

Commercial Roofing Clovis Businesses Can Actually Budget

Most commercial roofing decisions in Clovis come down to a spreadsheet, so here is the honest math. A tear-off-and-replace on a conventional system means demolition labor, dumpster and landfill fees, days of disruption, and a brand-new roof that starts deteriorating the day it is finished — with another tear-off waiting at the end of its life. A sprayed foam system installs over the existing roof in most cases, which deletes the demolition line entirely. New SPF installations run $4–$8 per square foot depending on foam thickness, roof complexity, and prep. More importantly, SPF changes the shape of the lifetime cost curve: when the protective coating weathers thin after 10 to 20 years, the roof is cleaned and recoated at $2–$4 per square foot instead of being replaced. The foam itself stays. Run that cycle out over thirty years for a 20,000-square-foot tilt-up in the Clovis Industrial Park and the difference against repeated single-ply replacement is not subtle. For a full breakdown of what drives the number on your specific building, see our spray foam roofing cost guide.

The second budget item is energy, and this is where Clovis buildings feel SPF immediately. Closed-cell roofing foam delivers roughly R-6.5 per inch. A typical two-inch application adds R-13 directly on top of the deck — on the outside of the building envelope, where it stops heat before it ever enters the structure. Business owners along the Herndon corridor running rooftop package units through a Valley summer routinely see cooling loads drop after a foam roof goes on, because the roof deck that used to radiate heat into the conditioned space all evening simply stops doing it.

How Spray Polyurethane Foam Actually Works

SPF is a two-component chemistry — an isocyanate and a polyol resin — combined at the spray gun under heat and pressure. The mixture reacts within seconds, expanding roughly thirtyfold and curing into rigid closed-cell foam that bonds tenaciously to concrete, metal, wood, and most existing roof membranes. Three properties make it a roof rather than just an insulation layer. First, the closed-cell structure is itself waterproof; the millions of sealed cells do not wick or absorb water the way fibrous insulation does. Second, the foam is fully adhered across every square inch, so there is no path for water to travel laterally beneath it — the failure mode that makes single-ply leaks so maddening to trace. Third, the foam is self-flashing: it expands around pipes, drains, HVAC curbs, skylights, and parapet transitions, which is exactly where 90 percent of conventional roof leaks originate.

Over the cured foam we apply a protective elastomeric coating — typically 100% silicone — with granules embedded where foot traffic warrants. The coating shields the foam from UV, takes the weathering hit, and is the renewable layer in the recoat cycle. The result is a roof assembly with no fasteners, no seams, no flashing details cut by hand, and no thermal bridges through the insulation. If you want the deeper engineering story, our spray polyurethane foam roofing overview covers the chemistry and assembly in detail.

From Old Town Storefronts to the Clovis Industrial Park

Clovis has a more varied flat-roof inventory than people assume. Old Town's retail blocks along Pollasky, Clovis Avenue, and Fifth Street are some of the oldest commercial buildings in Fresno County — brick parapet construction with flat roofs that have been patched, tarred, and re-patched for generations. These roofs are ideal foam candidates: SPF bridges the accumulated patchwork, seals the parapet-to-deck transitions that leak during every winter storm, and adds insulation that vintage buildings never had. The industrial park east of Clovis Avenue carries the opposite building stock — tilt-up concrete and steel-frame warehouses with large, open roof fields where foam's seamless coverage and insulation value pay off at scale.

Between those extremes sits the Herndon Avenue medical corridor around Clovis Community Medical Center: medical office buildings, imaging centers, and clinics where roof failure is not an inconvenience but a compliance and continuity problem. Foam application is fast, comparatively quiet, and staged to keep buildings occupied throughout — a real advantage for practices that cannot relocate patients while a roof crew works overhead. Add the strip retail along Shaw and Willow, church and school-support buildings across the city, and the new commercial pads following the Loma Vista and Heritage Grove growth toward Shepherd Avenue, and nearly every commercial roof in Clovis has a foam answer.

The Central Valley Climate Test

Roofing systems get sold on lab specs, but they fail in the field, and the eastern Fresno County field is uniquely demanding. Consider what a Clovis roof endures in a single year. Summer brings 40-plus days at or above 100°F, rooftop membrane temperatures that can exceed 160°F, and one of the highest annual UV doses in the country. Fall drops ag dust from harvest across every horizontal surface — fine sediment that clogs drains and holds moisture against membranes. Winter parks tule fog over the Valley floor for days, keeping roofs continuously damp between the storms that deliver most of the year's ten-to-twelve inches of rain in a three-month window. Spring winds coming down the Sierra foothills through the CA-168 corridor pry at loose edges and lift anything mechanically fastened.

SPF answers each stress directly. The foam is fully adhered, so wind uplift has no purchase point — a genuine consideration for buildings in the open northeast growth corridors. The silicone topcoat is UV-stable and does not chalk away in the sun the way acrylics do, and it sheds the winter damp without absorbing it. Ponding water, the chronic disease of aging Valley flat roofs, is often engineered out during application: because foam is applied as an expanding liquid, our installers build slope and crickets into low areas, restoring positive drainage that the original roof lost decades ago. No membrane system can do that without a full tapered-insulation redesign.

Reflectivity carries the summer half of the equation. A weathered dark roof in Clovis absorbs solar energy all afternoon and re-radiates it into the building well into the evening — which is why rooftop units keep running at 9 p.m. in August. The white silicone surface over foam reflects the majority of that load, and the foam beneath blocks what the coating does not reflect. Maintenance in this climate is refreshingly modest, but it is not zero, and we say so: fall drain clearing before the storm season, a rinse when harvest dust builds up enough to dull the reflective surface, and a periodic inspection so small coating wear gets touched up years before it matters. Owners who give a foam roof that minimal attention get the full recoat interval out of it; owners who ignore every roof equally at least start from a system with no seams to neglect.

Insulation Value and Title 24

California's Title 24 energy code makes roof performance a regulatory matter, not just a utility-bill matter, and reroofing projects can trigger insulation and cool-roof requirements. SPF is one of the cleanest compliance paths available for low-slope commercial work: the foam adds continuous insulation at roughly R-6.5 per inch with zero thermal bridging, and the white silicone topcoat delivers the high solar reflectance that cool-roof provisions call for. Instead of engineering rigid-board insulation, cover boards, and a membrane as separate layers, a single applied system handles insulation, waterproofing, and reflectivity together. We document foam thickness and coating specifications so your project file supports the permit, and because the insulation is on the exterior of the deck, conditioned space gains the benefit without losing an inch of interior clearance — something warehouse operators in the industrial park care about more than any R-value table.

There is a planning angle worth flagging for owners weighing timing. Reroofing projects that trigger Title 24 provisions can turn a simple membrane swap into an insulation upgrade project, with the cost stacking accordingly. SPF collapses that stack: the same application that waterproofs the roof supplies the continuous insulation and the reflective surface in one specification. For buildings changing hands, changing tenants, or heading into HVAC replacement — all common moments when energy documentation gets scrutinized in a growing market like Clovis — a foam roof puts the envelope numbers on the right side of the file before anyone asks for them.

Metal Building Roofing: Foam Over Aging Panels

Clovis and its satellites — Sanger's packing sheds, Friant's shop buildings, the contractor yards off Fowler and Sunnyside — run on metal buildings, and metal roofs have a predictable end-game: the fastener gaskets dry out, the panel laps loosen, rust blooms at the scratches, and every one of several thousand screw penetrations becomes a potential leak. Replacing panels is expensive and disruptive; screwing down a second skin adds thousands of new holes. Foam takes a different route entirely. Applied directly over the cleaned and primed panels, SPF encapsulates every fastener and lap seam in one monolithic layer, stops the oil-canning movement that backs screws out, kills the condensation drip that plagues uninsulated steel, and converts an R-nothing metal skin into an insulated roof assembly. The building gets quieter in the rain and dramatically cooler in July at the same time. For metal building owners weighing panel replacement against foam, the drone survey and core-sample assessment settles the question with data rather than guesswork.

Second, the recoat line is the one that matters most over time: a foam roof maintained on its 10-to-20-year recoat cycle never faces a tear-off again. Our Installation Process on a Clovis Roof

A foam project follows a disciplined sequence, and we keep owners informed at every stage. It begins with the free assessment: a drone survey of the full roof field, core sampling where deck saturation or hidden layers need confirming, and a written bid within 48 hours. On installation day the roof is cleaned and prepped — loose gravel removed, saturated areas cut out and dried, surfaces primed as the substrate requires. Foam application follows in controlled passes to the specified thickness, with our applicators building slope into ponding areas and flashing every penetration as they go. The silicone topcoat goes on once the foam has cured, with granule embedment at walk paths and around serviced equipment. We finish with a walkthrough, documentation of thicknesses and coatings for your records, and the maintenance guidance that keeps the system inside its warranty and recoat cycle. Most Clovis buildings stay open and operating for the duration; spray scheduling works around your hours where overspray control or odor-sensitive occupancies require it. The step-by-step detail is covered in our spray foam roofing installation guide.

Weather windows matter more in this trade than most, and we schedule around the Valley's calendar deliberately. Foam and coating application want dry substrates and workable temperatures, which makes late spring through fall the prime Clovis season — and makes the weeks before the November storm line the busiest. Owners who book assessments in late summer get first pick of the calendar; owners who call during the first atmospheric river of the season join a triage list. Neither gets a rushed application, because pass thickness and cure discipline are exactly the corners a schedule must never cut on a roof designed to outlast its coating cycle several times over.

Foam Against the Alternatives

Building owners comparing bids in the Fresno-Clovis market usually see SPF quoted against TPO, and the comparison deserves straight talk. TPO is a fine membrane installed by a fine crew — but it is a seamed, mechanically fastened system, and every seam is welded by hand on your roof, in Valley conditions, at whatever pace the schedule allows. Its insulation is a separate board layer bridged by thousands of fasteners, each one a small thermal short-circuit. SPF has no seams to weld and no fasteners to bridge; insulation and waterproofing are the same monolithic layer. TPO also cannot correct ponding without a tapered redesign, while foam builds drainage during application. Where TPO wins is a low upfront bid on a simple roof, and we say so when it is true. Our side-by-side spray foam vs TPO comparison walks through the trade-offs in detail, and our longevity data lives in how long spray foam roofing lasts.

That radius takes in the whole Fresno-Clovis metro: Fresno's commercial corridors to the west, Sanger's ag-industrial buildings to the southeast, and Friant's shops and facilities up by Millerton Lake to the north. silicone-roof-coating.body_html:
Silicone Roof Coating in Clovis: The Case for Restoration

Silicone roof coating gives Clovis building owners a third option between patching a tired roof forever and paying for a tear-off it may not need. Most flat roofs in eastern Fresno County do not fail structurally — they weather. The membrane surface chalks and craze-cracks under one of the highest UV loads in the country, seams and flashings open under summer heat cycling, and by year fifteen the roof leaks even though 90 percent of the assembly underneath is still sound. A 100% silicone coating system addresses exactly that situation: the existing roof is cleaned, repaired at its failure points, and sealed under a seamless, UV-immune, waterproof membrane at $2–$4 per square foot — typically a fraction of what replacement costs once demolition, disposal, and new material are counted. Allstate Spray Foam Roofing has been coating Central Valley roofs for more than twenty years as a family-owned, fully licensed contractor (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited and an SPFA member, with crews reaching Clovis from our Tulare County shop in about 55 minutes.

The timing question is the one that decides most coating projects, and it deserves plain language. A roof is a restoration candidate while its bones are still good — sound deck, mostly dry insulation, failures concentrated at seams, flashings, and the weathered surface. Wait too long and the window closes: water saturates the insulation field, the deck starts moving, and the only honest options left are sectional rebuilds or full replacement at several times the price. The frustrating part of this trade is meeting owners two winters after the coating window shut, holding repair invoices that add up to half a restoration and a roof that now needs the expensive answer anyway. The free assessment exists to put a date on your roof's window. A drone survey and a handful of core samples tell us — and you — whether this is a $2-per-foot year, a $4-per-foot year, or a year to budget for something bigger, and the written bid arrives within 48 hours either way.

What a 100% Silicone Membrane Actually Does

Not all coatings are close cousins, and the distinction matters in this climate. Acrylic coatings are water-based; they re-emulsify under standing water and wear thin under UV, which makes them a poor match for Valley roofs that pond through the winter and bake through the summer. Asphaltic coatings dry out and crack on the same cycle that killed the original roof. High-solids 100% silicone is a different chemistry: it is moisture-cure, meaning humidity helps rather than hurts it; it is permanently UV-stable, so Fresno County's 260-plus sunny days cannot chalk it away; and it tolerates ponding water indefinitely — the single property that separates it from nearly everything else in the coating aisle. Applied at proper millage over a prepared surface, it forms a seamless rubber-like membrane that moves with the roof through 100-degree heat swings without splitting, and its bright white surface reflects the solar load that used to pour through the deck into your conditioned space.

Application quality is where identical materials produce opposite outcomes, so the specification matters as much as the chemistry. A proper system is applied in measured millage — typically two passes on a first-time restoration — with wet-film thickness checked during application rather than guessed afterward. Details are done first and by hand: seams get reinforcement where movement demands it, fasteners get individually capped on metal roofs, and flashings get brush-grade material worked into the transition before any field coating flows. Walk paths and equipment surrounds get granules embedded into the final coat, solving silicone's one genuine handling drawback — its slickness when wet — exactly where people actually walk. Every one of those line items appears in our written bid, because a coating quote that only states a price and a color is hiding the variables that determine whether the membrane lasts eight years or eighteen.

Roof Coating for Clovis Buildings That Cannot Close

The buildings that benefit most from coating are the ones that can least afford replacement disruption, and Clovis is full of them. A tear-off means dumpsters in the parking lot, days of noise and debris, and sections of the building exposed to weather mid-project. A silicone restoration is quiet by comparison: cleaning, targeted repairs, and roller- or spray-applied coating, with the building open and operating underneath the entire time. That difference is decisive for the medical and dental offices clustered along Herndon Avenue near Clovis Community Medical Center, where patient schedules do not pause for roofing. It matters for the Old Town retail blocks along Pollasky and Clovis Avenue, where a shared roof spans several storefronts and no tenant wants to be the one closed during an event weekend. It matters for the schools, churches, and gyms scattered across the city, which need summer-window work that actually finishes inside the summer window. Coating projects compress the calendar in a way replacement never can.

Silicone Flat Roof Coating Over Every Common Substrate

Silicone's versatility across substrates is what makes it the workhorse of roof restoration. Over spray polyurethane foam, silicone is the standard protective layer — every SPF roof carries a coating, and recoating on schedule is what makes a foam roof effectively permanent (the full system story is in our spray polyurethane foam roofing guide). Over single-ply membranes like TPO and EPDM, silicone seals the seams and flashings that are the membrane's chronic weak points, buying a decade or more from a roof whose field material is still serviceable. Over modified bitumen and built-up roofs — the dominant stock on Clovis's older commercial buildings — silicone locks down alligatored, oxidized surfaces before they crack through. And over metal panels, covered in depth below, it solves the fastener-and-seam leak pattern that plagues every aging steel roof in the Valley. The free assessment tells us which situation your roof is in: drone survey of the field, core sampling where saturation is suspected, written bid within 48 hours.

One substrate note saves Clovis owners real money: mixed roofs. Older commercial buildings that have been added onto over the decades — common in Old Town and along the original arterials — often carry two or three different roof systems meeting at awkward transitions, and those transitions are reliably where the leaks live. Because silicone adheres across all of the common substrates, a single restoration can unify a mixed roof under one continuous membrane, eliminating the transition details that no patching program ever permanently solves. It is one of the quiet places where a coating outperforms even a partial replacement, which would simply create a new transition to leak.

Pros and Cons — the Honest Version

We sell coatings nearly every week, and we still tell owners the whole truth about them, because a coating applied to the wrong roof fails and takes our name with it. The genuine advantages: silicone costs a fraction of replacement at $2–$4 per square foot; there is no tear-off, no landfill load, and minimal disruption; it handles ponding water and UV better than any competing chemistry; the white surface cuts summer cooling loads; and it is renewable — when it weathers thin in 10 to 20 years, you recoat again rather than replace. The honest limitations: silicone is slick when wet, so designated walk paths get granule embedment; it holds dirt and dulls over time, which affects looks more than performance but is worth knowing; once a roof is siliconed, future work must also be silicone, because almost nothing else adheres to it; and — most important — a coating is a restoration, not a resurrection. A roof with widespread saturated insulation, rotten decking, or structural issues needs those areas cut out and rebuilt, or needs a new roof entirely, and our core samples will say so before we quote a coating that should not happen.

Silicone Roof Coating Cost and Price in Clovis

Silicone roof coating price questions deserve real numbers, so here are the ranges Clovis projects actually land in and what pushes a roof up or down within them.

Within the range, three variables do most of the work: surface preparation (a chalked, dirty roof needs washing and priming; a recent foam roof needs little), repair scope (open seams, wet insulation cut-outs, flashing rebuilds), and millage specification (more coating thickness costs more and lasts longer — we quote the thickness, not just the price, so bids compare honestly). A cheap coating bid that is silent about millage is usually a thin coating, and a thin coating in Fresno County sun is a short one.

Metal Roof Coating: Fasteners, Seams, and Rust

Metal roofs earn their own section because Clovis's satellite economy runs on them — the packing and processing buildings around Sanger, the shop buildings out toward Friant, the contractor yards and light-industrial steel of the Clovis Industrial Park. An aging metal roof leaks in a completely predictable pattern: thousands of fastener gaskets dry-rot on the same schedule, panel laps loosen as the steel oil-cans through daily heat cycles, and rust establishes at every scratch and low spot. Coating that roof is a system, not a paint job. We wash the panels, treat rust, detail every fastener head and lap seam with brush-grade silicone or seam tape, then flood-coat the field to specification. The result seals all several thousand penetrations at once, stops the leak chase for good, and drops the panel temperature dramatically in summer — steel that ran too hot to touch in July reflects most of that load instead. For an occupied shop or warehouse, it is the difference between a working roof and a re-roofing project the business cannot schedule.

Warehouses, Schools, and the Summer Work Window

Two Clovis building categories deserve their own scheduling notes. Warehouses and distribution space — the industrial park's stock in trade — benefit from coating precisely because their roofs are huge: at 30,000 square feet, the per-foot difference between restoration and replacement is not a rounding error, it is a capital decision. Large fields also coat efficiently, which pushes big simple roofs toward the friendly end of the $2–$4 range. The operational note is dust and heat: we schedule around receiving hours and skip application during the worst of harvest-season particulate so the membrane cures clean.

Schools, churches, and institutional buildings run on the opposite constraint — the calendar. A campus roof project in one of the Valley's largest school communities has a hard window between June and August, and a coating project actually fits it: no tear-off phase, no exposed deck gambling on a surprise thunderstorm, no demolition debris where students return in weeks. Church campuses along the older avenues and gymnasium roofs across town follow the same logic on Sunday-to-Sunday and season-to-season rhythms. We build these schedules backward from the immovable date, stage the work in sections so any single day's weather risk is contained, and hand facilities staff the millage documentation their maintenance file — and their board — wants to see. It is unglamorous project management, and it is exactly why institutional roofs are some of our steadiest Clovis work.

Ponding Water and the Clovis Winter

Clovis gets nearly all of its ten-to-twelve inches of annual rain between November and March, often in concentrated storm systems coming up the Valley — which means a flat roof spends the wet season being tested precisely where it is weakest. Ponding is the classic failure accelerant: water collects in deflected bays and around clogged drains, and whatever coating or membrane sits under that pond degrades fastest. Two facts matter here. First, 100% silicone is the one mainstream coating chemistry that genuinely tolerates permanent ponding — it will not re-emulsify or blister under standing water the way acrylics do. Second, tolerance is not an excuse for bad drainage: during prep we clear and resettle drains, and where ponds are deep or structural, we quote foam build-up to restore slope rather than coating over a lake and calling it solved. Between storms, tule fog keeps roofs damp for days at a time; silicone's moisture-cure chemistry shrugs at that, but the prep windows matter, which is one more reason coating season in the Valley is best scheduled before the fog settles in.

Drainage stewardship continues after we leave, and we are direct with owners about their half of the bargain. A coated roof sheds water beautifully, but no membrane can drain through a scupper packed with cottonwood leaves or a drain basket buried in harvest dust. The maintenance ask is small — clear the drains before the first November system, glance at them after each big storm, keep rooftop trades from leaving debris — and it protects both the roof and the guarantee behind it. Where a building has a history of drain problems, we say so in the assessment and, where the structure allows, add overflow protection to the scope, because the cheapest insurance against a ceiling collapse is a second way off the roof for water.

The Recoat Cycle: How 10 to 20 Years Becomes Forever

The most misunderstood number in this business is coating life. A silicone membrane weathers gradually — it does not fail on a birthday. Depending on millage, sun exposure, and foot traffic, the coating serves 10 to 20 years before it thins to the point of needing renewal, and renewal is the whole point: clean the surface, repair any incidental damage, apply new silicone, and the clock resets at $2–$4 per square foot. On a foam roof, this cycle is what makes the system effectively permanent — the foam never sees daylight, so it never degrades, and only the sacrificial coating layer is ever replaced. Owners who internalize this stop thinking about their roof as a depreciating asset with a demolition date and start budgeting it like scheduled maintenance, which is exactly what it becomes. The long-run math is laid out in how long spray foam roofing lasts, and it is the strongest argument for getting a restorable roof under coating before it deteriorates past the restoration threshold.

Between recoats, the system asks very little, but a light inspection rhythm pays for itself. We recommend a roof check twice a year — once after the storm season ends in spring, once before it begins in fall — plus a look after any rooftop trade work, because HVAC and solar crews cause more coating damage in this Valley than weather does. Small punctures and cuts caught early are trivial silicone repairs; the same damage left through a winter becomes a wet-insulation cut-out. Owners who want it handled entirely can put the building on our inspection calendar, and either way the drone makes the survey fast, thorough, and documented.

How We Coat a Roof in Clovis

Every coating project follows the same disciplined arc. It starts with the free assessment — drone survey of the entire field, moisture readings and core samples where the story is uncertain, and a written bid within 48 hours that specifies substrate condition, repair scope, and coating millage. Project day one is preparation: pressure washing, drain clearing, cutting out and drying any saturated sections found in the survey. Detail work follows — every seam, fastener, flashing, curb, and penetration gets hand-treatment before a drop of field coating goes down, because coatings fail at details, not in the field. Then the flood coat is applied to specification, with granule-embedded walk paths at rooftop equipment and access routes. We close with a final inspection, documented millage readings, and maintenance guidance — mostly keeping drains clear through the November-to-March storm season and calling us rather than a handyman if rooftop trades cut into the membrane. Buildings stay occupied throughout; silicone application is low-odor and staged around your operating hours where needed.

Season and weather get managed, not wished away. Silicone's moisture-cure chemistry gives it more scheduling tolerance than most coatings, but application still wants a clean, dry surface and a rain-free cure window — which in practice makes late spring through mid-fall the natural Clovis coating season and makes September the smartest month on the calendar: past the worst heat, ahead of the first storms, with the roof's summer damage fully visible to the survey. Fog-season work is possible on the right roof with the right windows, but we would rather tell you to wait ninety days than apply a membrane into conditions that shortchange its cure.

Why Allstate for Your Clovis Roof Coating

Coating is an unforgiving trade dressed up as an easy one — anyone can buy a drum of silicone, and every summer somebody in the Valley learns why millage specs, moisture readings, and detail work exist. Our advantage is that coatings are not a sideline: as an SPF contractor, protecting roofs with silicone is half of everything we have done for twenty-plus years, and our crews carry that repetition onto every Clovis roof. We quote from core-sample evidence, we specify thickness in writing, we stand behind the work with industry-leading leak-proof guarantees, and if your roof is past the point where a coating is honest, we say so and price the alternative. One call to (559) 739-9519 starts the free drone assessment for any building in Clovis, Fresno, Sanger, or Friant — and 48 hours later you will know exactly what your roof needs and what it costs.

And if the assessment finds a roof still years from needing us, we will tell you that too, with the photos to prove it. A contractor who quotes every roof he surveys is running a sales funnel, not an inspection. The drone imagery goes in your file either way, the baseline makes every future decision easier, and when your roof's restoration window does open, you will already know who measured it honestly.

Roof Repair Clovis Property Owners Can Actually Trust

Roof repair in Clovis usually starts the same way: a stain spreads across a ceiling tile during the first real November storm, someone puts a bucket under it, and the search begins for a contractor who will fix the roof instead of selling a new one. That is the call we built this service around. Allstate Spray Foam Roofing repairs flat, low-slope, foam, and metal roofs across Clovis and the surrounding Fresno County communities — leaks, ponding, blisters, split seams, failed flashings, and storm damage — as a family-owned contractor with more than twenty years in Central Valley roofing, CA License #C-2-1052735, BBB accreditation, and SPFA membership. No mystery invoices, no repairs that are really down payments on a replacement pitch.

The people who call us are as varied as the roofs. Property managers running multi-tenant retail along Shaw and Willow need documentation and predictable scheduling as much as workmanship. Small business owners in Old Town need straight answers about whether the building they lease or own justifies another repair. Facilities staff at medical offices, churches, and schools need work performed around occupancy without surprises. And owners of flat-roofed and foam-roofed homes — a real population in the older Fresno-Clovis neighborhoods — need a contractor who treats a modest residential flat roof with the same diagnostic rigor as a warehouse. All of them get the identical process, because the process is the product: survey the whole roof, prove the diagnosis, put the fix and the price in writing, and stand behind the result with industry-leading leak-proof guarantees.

Flat Roof Repair Across the Fresno-Clovis Metro

Flat and low-slope roofs dominate Clovis's commercial stock, and they fail differently than the pitched shingle roofs most repair advice is written for. On a pitched roof, water runs off; on a flat roof, water lingers, probes, and finds the one detail that summer heat opened up. The repair inventory we see most across the metro: seams and laps split by thermal cycling on built-up and modified bitumen roofs; flashings pulled away from parapets and curbs; punctures and tears from rooftop equipment service; drains and scuppers clogged by fall leaf-drop and harvest dust until water finds another way down; and coatings worn through at walk paths and equipment surrounds. Each of these has a right repair and several wrong ones. Mastic smeared over a wet seam is a wrong one — it holds until the next heat cycle, then fails in the same storm season it was meant to survive. Our repairs cut out the failure, dry the substrate, and rebuild the detail with materials matched to the roof, which is why they hold through the following winter rather than through the following month.

Material matching is the unglamorous half of a repair that lasts. A TPO roof wants heat-welded TPO details, not a smear of universal sealant; a modified bitumen roof wants compatible mod-bit or a properly primed liquid flashing; a coated roof wants the same coating chemistry it already carries, because almost nothing bonds to silicone except silicone. We stock our repair rigs accordingly, and it is a genuine difference between a flat-roof specialist and a general roofer whose truck is set up for shingles. The wrong material on the right spot is still the wrong repair — it just takes one more storm season to prove it.

Foam Roof Repair Done the Way Foam Should Be Repaired

Clovis has a growing population of SPF roofs, and foam repair is its own discipline — one general roofers regularly get wrong. Foam roofs rarely leak in the field; they get damaged at specific points: a dropped tool or hail strike punching the coating, a trade cutting into the roof for a conduit run, birds pecking at an exposed edge, or simply a coating reaching the thin end of its 10-to-20-year cycle. The correct repair is straightforward for a foam contractor: cut out the damaged foam, dry the area, fill with new foam or a compatible sealant, and re-coat with silicone to spec. The incorrect repairs we get called to undo are depressingly consistent — asphalt products smeared onto foam (they attack it), incompatible coatings that never bond, or screwed-down metal patches that add the very penetrations foam exists to eliminate. As the Valley's foam specialists, we repair SPF with SPF-correct methods, and if your foam roof was installed by someone else and never maintained, our foam roof repair service covers the full restoration path from spot repairs to complete recoat.

Finding the Leak: Why Flat Roofs Fool Everyone

The hardest part of flat roof repair is not the fix — it is the find. Water that enters at a parapet crack on the north side can travel laterally along the deck, under insulation, across a beam, and appear as a ceiling stain forty feet from the actual breach. This is why handyman patches so often fail: they seal the spot above the drip, not the hole in the roof. Our diagnostic sequence is built to beat that geometry. The drone survey maps the whole field first — ponding rings, coating wear, suspect seams, displaced flashings — so nothing is diagnosed through a keyhole. Moisture readings and core samples then confirm what is wet and what is dry, tracing the water back to its entry rather than its exit. On seamless foam roofs this lateral-travel problem barely exists, because the fully adhered foam gives water no path to wander — one of the quiet reasons owners who get tired of chronic leak-chasing eventually convert to SPF (the system is described in our spray polyurethane foam roofing guide).

Ponding Water: The Repair That Prevents the Next Five

Stand on almost any aging flat roof in Clovis a day after a winter storm and you will find the ponds — shallow lakes over deflected bays, around settled drains, behind equipment curbs. Ponding is not cosmetic. Standing water accelerates whatever weakness sits beneath it, multiplies the load on the structure, breeds the algae and debris that clog drains further, and in a hard freeze — which the Valley floor does get on clear winter nights — it becomes an ice lens working at every crack. Most repair contractors can only treat the symptom, because fixing ponding on a membrane roof means re-engineering slope. Foam gives us a better tool: because SPF is applied as an expanding liquid, we build up low areas and shape crickets around drains and curbs, restoring positive drainage as part of the repair itself. It is the single highest-leverage flat roof repair in this climate, because it removes the condition that was busy manufacturing your next three leaks.

Storm Damage and Response — an Honest Word

When a Pacific storm system trains up the Valley and the wind comes down off the Sierra through the 168 corridor, the phones get busy, so here is our honest framing rather than an invented promise. We are 55 minutes away, we prioritize active leaks over scheduled maintenance, and we will tell you on the phone — truthfully — when a crew can be on your roof. What we will not do is advertise a response-time guarantee we cannot control the weather or the queue well enough to keep. What we can do fast is triage: temporary waterproofing to stop active water entry, drone documentation of the damage for your records and your insurer, and a written repair scope within 48 hours so the permanent fix is scheduled before the next system arrives. Wind-lifted edge metal, peeled flashings, equipment blown into membranes, and debris punctures are the standard post-storm inventory, and all of it repairs faster when the documentation is done right the first day.

On insurance itself, our role is evidence, not advocacy theater. The drone survey produces a dated, comprehensive visual record of the roof — before-and-after where we did the temporary work — and our written scope separates storm damage from pre-existing wear honestly, because inflated claims help nobody and accurate ones settle faster. Owners who had an assessment on file before the storm are in the strongest position of all: a documented baseline turns the damage conversation from opinion into comparison. It is one more argument for the free fall survey, and it costs nothing to have in the drawer.

Maintenance: The Cheapest Roof Repair Is the One You Never Need

A striking share of the repair calls we run in Clovis were preventable for less than the deductible. The killers are mundane: drains and scuppers that stopped draining, coating wear at walk paths that nobody walked in years, a satellite installer's lag bolts through the membrane, seams that telegraphed their failure a full season before they opened. A twice-a-year inspection rhythm — after the storms in spring, before them in fall — catches essentially all of it while it is still trivial to fix. For owners who want the discipline without the ladder, we put buildings on a scheduled drone-survey calendar: same flight pattern each visit, changes flagged against the prior imagery, small fixes quoted in writing before they become winter emergencies. Multi-building owners and property managers get the most leverage from this — one scheduled afternoon covers a portfolio — but even a single Old Town storefront benefits from having its roof's history documented instead of remembered. The economics are not subtle: the average preventive fix we quote is a fraction of the average emergency invoice, and it gets scheduled in September sunshine instead of performed in a January storm break.

What We See on Clovis Roofs, Corridor by Corridor

Twenty years in the Valley teaches you that roof problems cluster by building stock. In Old Town Clovis, the brick retail blocks along Pollasky and Clovis Avenue carry flat roofs with decades of layered patches; the chronic issues are parapet flashings, dead-level drainage, and roofs where the honest question is whether one more patch is money well spent — we answer with core data, not a sales script. Along the Herndon medical corridor near Clovis Community Medical Center, the buildings are newer but the stakes are higher: single-ply roofs over occupied clinical space, where a small seam failure becomes a compliance problem, and where our low-disruption repair scheduling matters as much as the workmanship. In the Clovis Industrial Park and the metal-building yards off Fowler and Sunnyside, the pattern is fastener-gasket failure and panel-lap leaks by the thousand — spot-repairable early, coating-scale later. And in the newer northeast retail pads toward Loma Vista, we mostly see construction-era details failing early: pitch pockets, HVAC curbs, and penetrations that were flashed in a hurry during the building boom.

Schools, churches, and civic buildings form their own category across a city defined by its campuses. These roofs are usually large, usually flat or barely pitched, and usually maintained on public or congregation budgets that reward early, small repairs over deferred large ones. We work their calendars — summer windows for the big work, holiday breaks for the middle-sized, and quiet weekday scheduling for anything urgent — and we document everything, because facilities committees change and paper outlasts memory. The same applies to the mini-storage rows and small industrial condos multiplying along the growth corridors: modest roofs, absentee owners, and a repair model that runs on clear photos and written scopes rather than site meetings.

Repair or Replace? A Straight Answer in 48 Hours

Every owner eventually faces the fork: keep repairing, or invest in a new system. We put the decision on paper with evidence. As a rule of thumb, a roof with localized damage, dry insulation, and a sound deck should be repaired; a roof with widespread saturation, repeated failures across the field, or a deck problem should be restored or replaced, because repairs on a failing field are rent, not equity.

Roof conditionRight moveTypical economics
Localized damage, dry cores, sound fieldTargeted repairLowest cost; restores full service life of existing roof
Sound structure, weathered surface, scattered failuresSilicone restoration or SPF overlayRecoat $2–$4/sq ft; new foam system $4–$8/sq ft — no tear-off
Widespread saturation or deck failureReplacement of affected areas or full systemHighest cost; repairs here only postpone and compound

The core samples make this call honest. Saturated insulation does not dry out on its own, and it tells us — and you — exactly how far gone a roof is. If your roof lands in the middle row, the restoration path usually wins the math decisively; our spray foam roofing cost guide lays out what the overlay numbers look like at your square footage.

What a Repair Visit Looks Like

From the first call to the finished fix, the sequence is designed so you always know what is happening and why. First, the assessment — free, and the same rigor whether the job turns out to be a $900 flashing repair or a full restoration: drone survey of the complete roof field, moisture readings, core samples where needed. Second, the written scope within 48 hours: what failed, why, what we will do about it, and the price. Third, the repair itself — failure cut out rather than covered over, substrate dried, detail rebuilt with compatible materials, and the surrounding area inspected for the same failure mode, because defects that show in one curb are usually incubating in the others. Finally, documentation: photos of the completed work and any watch-items we found for your file. Buildings stay open throughout; we stage around business hours, patient schedules, and school calendars as the site requires, and we leave the roof cleaner than the leak left your ceiling.

One expectation worth setting: a right-sized repair sometimes reveals a bigger story, and we handle that moment with candor rather than escalation theater. If the cut-out shows saturation spreading beyond the visible failure, we photograph it, complete the contracted repair correctly, and give you the finding in writing with options — more exploratory cores, a monitored watch, or a restoration quote — rather than parking a change order on your desk mid-job. Owners keep working with contractors who tell them the truth at the awkward moment; that has been our experience for twenty years, and it is cheaper for everyone than discovering the same saturation through a collapsed ceiling tile two winters later.

Heat, Fog, and Why Clovis Roofs Crack on Schedule

It helps to understand the machine that is breaking your roof, because it runs on a calendar. Summer in Clovis delivers weeks above 100°F; a dark roof surface hits 160°F by afternoon and sheds forty-plus degrees overnight, and that daily expansion-contraction cycle works every seam, fastener, and flashing like a wire being bent back and forth. Autumn adds harvest dust from the ag country east toward Sanger — fine sediment that dams scuppers and holds moisture against the membrane. Then winter inverts the whole system: tule fog seals the Valley floor under a damp lid for days at a time, so the moisture summer let in never dries out, and the season's ten-to-twelve inches of rain arrive concentrated in exactly the months the roof is weakest. The practical takeaway is timing: the cheapest repair you will ever buy is the one done in September and October, after the heat has done its damage and before the storm season audits it. A fall drone survey costs you nothing and regularly saves Clovis owners the January emergency call.

Elevation adds a wrinkle on the east side of town. As Clovis climbs toward the Sierra foothills along the 168 corridor, buildings pick up more wind exposure than the sheltered valley floor, and the occasional cold snap bites harder — clear-night frosts that turn yesterday's pond into this morning's ice lens. Roofs out toward the foothill margins earn their fall inspection twice over, and anything mechanically fastened or loosely flashed up there should be checked after every significant wind event, not just annually. Meanwhile the older, lower parts of town fight the opposite micro-battle: mature street trees that fill scuppers with leaf-drop precisely when the first storms arrive. Same city, two different maintenance calendars — and one more reason a repair contractor should know the local map, not just the trade.

Serving Clovis, Fresno, Sanger, and Friant

Our repair crews cover the whole northeast Fresno County market from the Tulare County shop — about 55 minutes to Clovis via Highway 99 and CA-168, with Fresno's commercial corridors, Sanger's packing and ag-industrial buildings, and Friant's facilities up by Millerton Lake inside the same service radius. We are straightforward about the geography: no Clovis storefront, no pretense of one — just a specialist crew that has been working Fresno County flat roofs for two decades and stands behind every repair with industry-leading leak-proof guarantees. If water is coming in now, call (559) 739-9519 and we will tell you honestly when we can be there. If the roof is merely worrying you, book the free assessment: drone survey, core samples where warranted, and a written answer in 48 hours about what your roof actually needs — repair, restoration, or nothing yet.

That last option is not a throwaway line. A meaningful share of the assessments we fly in Clovis end with us telling the owner their roof is fine — a drain to clear, a watch-item to photograph again next fall, nothing to invoice. We can afford that honesty because the specialty sustains itself: the owners whose roofs genuinely need work keep our crews busy year-round, and the owners whose roofs do not become the ones who call us first when that changes. Twenty years in the same Valley teaches a simple lesson about repair work — the diagnosis is the reputation, and the reputation is the business. Put ours to the test on your building.

The climate one-two punch: 100-degree summer heat cycling splits seams and flashings, then the November-through-March storm season and weeks of tule fog exploit every opening while the roof stays too damp to dry out. Commercial Spray Foam Insulation for Clovis Businesses

Commercial spray foam insulation solves a problem most Clovis building owners have simply learned to live with: steel and concrete shells that are brutal to occupy in July and clammy through the tule-fog months, with utility bills that reflect the fact the building has effectively no thermal envelope at all. A bare metal building on the Valley floor is a heat exchanger — the skin hits well over 140°F under summer sun and pours that load straight into the workspace, then reverses the trade on winter nights, sweating condensation onto everything below. Closed-cell spray polyurethane foam, applied directly to the interior of the roof deck and walls, converts that skin into an insulated, air-sealed, moisture-controlled envelope in a single application — roughly R-6.5 per inch, fully adhered, with no gaps, sags, or thermal bridges. Allstate Spray Foam Roofing has applied commercial foam across the Central Valley for more than twenty years as a family-owned, fully licensed contractor (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited and an SPFA member. Our crews reach Clovis from our Tulare County shop in about 55 minutes, and we work commercial exclusively — metal buildings, warehouses, cold storage, and shop space are the lane, and we stay in it.

The calls come from every corner of the commercial map. Owners of shop buildings who are tired of losing the afternoon to heat. General contractors closing out metal-building projects that need envelope numbers for the permit file. Property managers with a tilt-up whose tenants complain from both ends of the thermostat. Packing and processing operators whose refrigeration bills climb every summer. Warehouse operators discovering that the fiberglass blanket their building came with has been soaking, sagging, and feeding pests for a decade. The common denominator is a building that was never really finished — a structure without an envelope — and a single-application fix that finishes it. Because the same closed-cell chemistry is also our roofing product, we are often solving both sides of the same building's problem in one mobilization: foam above the deck as the roof, foam below it as the envelope.

Closed-Cell Foam: What R-6.5 Per Inch Buys You

Closed-cell SPF is the highest-performing insulation commonly available, and the number that headlines it — approximately R-6.5 per inch — understates the advantage. Fibrous insulation achieves its rated R-value only under laboratory conditions: perfectly installed, uncompressed, dry, and with zero air movement. Real buildings deliver none of those conditions, and air infiltration alone can cut fibrous performance dramatically. Closed-cell foam does not depend on stillness because it creates it: the foam is its own air barrier, bonded to the substrate across every square inch, so the rated R-value is the delivered R-value. The closed-cell structure also refuses to absorb moisture — decisive in a fog climate — and adds rigidity to metal panels, measurably stiffening a steel building's skin. Two inches on a warehouse roof deck delivers R-13 of continuous insulation plus a complete air seal; three inches reaches roughly R-19.5. For most Clovis metal buildings, the difference between before and after is not a percentage on a bill — it is whether the space is usable at 3 p.m. in August.

The air-sealing half of the story deserves equal billing in this county, because Valley air carries more than heat. Harvest season loads the atmosphere east of town with fine agricultural dust, and an unsealed metal building breathes that dust through every panel lap and fastener hole, filming inventory, equipment, and product with sediment that no janitorial budget defeats. Foam closes the envelope against it the same way it closes it against heat — by eliminating the pathways rather than filtering the flow. Shops that foam their buildings notice the change in weeks: less dust on the benches, fewer insects finding their way in, a building that holds its conditioned air instead of trading it with the outdoors several times an hour. For food-adjacent businesses and clean-sensitive operations, the sealed envelope is frequently worth more than the R-value that comes with it.

Metal Buildings and the Clovis Industrial Park

The Clovis Industrial Park east of Clovis Avenue, the contractor yards off Sunnyside and Fowler, and the steel buildings scattered from Sanger's packing districts to the shops out toward Friant share the same construction DNA: pre-engineered metal buildings with, at best, sagging vinyl-faced fiberglass blankets pinched between purlins and panels. That blanket system fails in every way that matters here. Compression at every purlin cuts its real R-value to a fraction of the label. The vinyl facing tears, and the exposed fiberglass drinks the condensation the panels produce. Birds and pests nest in it. And it does nothing to stop air exchange through the thousand fastener holes and panel laps of a steel skin. Spray foam replaces the whole failed assembly in one pass: applied to the underside of the roof panels and walls, it fills the purlin cavities, encapsulates the fasteners, air-seals the laps, and delivers continuous R-value with no compression points. The building gets quieter, stiffer, dryer, and dramatically cheaper to condition — and for owners running evaporative coolers or oversized package units to brute-force the heat problem, the equipment downsizing at replacement time is part of the payback.

Cold Storage and Temperature-Controlled Space

Fresno County's economy moves perishables, and the cold chain runs on insulation. Sanger's fruit packing operations, processors across the metro, and the cold rooms behind Clovis's food businesses all fight the same physics: every BTU that leaks through the envelope is compressor runtime, and in a Valley summer the temperature differential across a cooler wall can exceed 65 degrees for weeks. Closed-cell foam is the standard answer in cold storage for reasons beyond raw R-value. Its air-sealing eliminates the infiltration that loads refrigeration hardest; its closed-cell structure is a vapor retarder in its own right, controlling the moisture drive that destroys lesser insulation at cold-wall interfaces; and it goes on seamlessly around the penetrations, hangers, and transitions where board insulation leaves joints. We insulate new cold rooms, upgrade existing ones, and — a Central Valley specialty — bring older packing and storage buildings up to the performance their refrigeration contractor wishes they had. Freezer and cooler work is scheduled around product and production; foam application is fast, and downtime is measured in shifts, not weeks.

Sanger, Friant, and the Ag-Building Belt

The satellite towns in our Clovis service radius run on agricultural steel, and their buildings work harder than almost anything inside the city limits. Sanger's packing houses, equipment barns, and processing support buildings cycle between summer heat that punishes workers and product, and fog-season damp that corrodes everything a roof panel drips on. Friant's shops and facility buildings up toward Millerton Lake add wind exposure and the wider temperature swings of the foothill margin. For both, closed-cell foam is less an upgrade than a structural correction: it stiffens wind-worked panels, stops the condensation that rusts buildings from the inside out, and makes seasonal workspaces usable across more of the year without heroic HVAC.

Ag operations also bring scheduling realities that a commercial insulation contractor either respects or fails. Harvest and packing seasons are untouchable; the work happens in the shoulder months or not at all. Buildings often cannot be fully emptied, so we mask, phase, and stage around equipment that stays. And budgets answer to commodity years, which is why our bids itemize thickness options honestly — the two-inch condensation-and-comfort spec versus the three-inch conditioned-space spec — so an operator can buy the performance the year affords and add to it later. Foam is one of the few insulation systems that genuinely accepts a phased approach: a second lift bonds to the first without seams or waste.

Spray Foam vs Fiberglass in Commercial Buildings

The comparison every owner asks for deserves a straight table rather than adjectives. Both materials insulate; the difference is what else each one does, and fails to do, in a Valley steel building.

Fiberglass keeps winning specifications on one axis only: first cost. In a mild climate with a framed, sheathed building, that can be a defensible trade. In an unconditioned steel box on the Fresno County valley floor — 100-degree summers, fog-season condensation, ag dust working through every unsealed lap — it is a purchase that keeps costing money every month it remains installed.

Owners sometimes ask about the middle options — rigid board, reflective bubble products, blown cellulose in framed sections — and each has a niche, none of it here. Board insulation on the underside of a metal roof fights the purlin geometry and leaves air paths at every joint; reflective barriers address radiant gain only and do nothing for air sealing or condensation; cellulose has no business near a fog-season steel skin. The reason closed-cell foam keeps winning Valley metal buildings is not marketing — it is that one material does all four jobs the building actually needs done: insulation, air barrier, vapor control, and panel stiffening. Any alternative requires assembling three or four products to match it, installed perfectly, in a building geometry that punishes assembly.

What Commercial Spray Foam Costs Per Square Foot

Commercial insulation pricing turns on three variables: foam thickness (driven by your target R-value and Title 24 requirements), substrate preparation (a new build sprays clean; a retrofit may need old blanket insulation stripped and panels prepped), and project geometry (open warehouse ceilings spray efficiently; cut-up spaces with racking, equipment, and lifts in place take staging). Because those variables swing widely, we quote from a site visit rather than publishing a misleading single number — but the structure of the bid is always transparent: square footage, specified thickness and resulting R-value, prep scope, and staging plan, in writing within 48 hours of the assessment. For context on how foam pricing behaves at commercial scale — and why thickness is the honest lever rather than the place bids quietly cut corners — our spray foam cost guide covers the economics in depth. The short version: foam costs more than fiberglass on day one and less than fiberglass every month after, and in this climate the crossover comes fast.

Title 24 and the Retrofit Trigger

California's Title 24 energy code shapes commercial insulation decisions in two directions. New construction and major renovations in Clovis must meet prescriptive envelope requirements, and closed-cell foam's continuous insulation — no thermal bridging through framing, no compression losses — makes compliance straightforward to demonstrate and document. But the code also reaches existing buildings more often than owners expect: alterations, changes of occupancy, and significant HVAC replacements can trigger envelope requirements, and an uninsulated metal building that was grandfathered for decades suddenly needs a real thermal envelope before the project closes out. Foam is frequently the only practical retrofit path in those cases, because it installs against the existing skin without reframing, furring, or losing usable interior volume. We document installed thickness and R-value for your compliance file, and we coordinate with your design-build or mechanical contractor so the envelope numbers and the equipment sizing tell the same story to the plan checker.

The paperwork side is easy to underrate until a project stalls on it. Our bids state the foam product, the installed thickness, and the resulting R-value in writing, and our completion documentation records what actually went on the steel — measured, not assumed. For owner-builders and small GCs navigating a Fresno County permit on a metal building, that file is the difference between a smooth final and a re-inspection; for owners who never pull a permit at all, it is the record that travels with the building when it sells or refinances. Either way, an insulation project that cannot document itself is worth less than it cost, and we treat the documentation as part of the product.

Condensation: The Tule Fog Problem Nobody Budgets For

Ask any Clovis shop owner about winter and you will hear about the drip. On clear nights the Valley floor radiates heat to the sky and metal roof panels drop below the dew point; when the tule fog settles in — as it does for days at a stretch between November and February — the entire building skin sits at saturation. Inside an uninsulated steel building, that means condensation raining off the purlins onto inventory, equipment, and stored materials, rusting the fasteners from the inside, and soaking whatever fiberglass was supposed to be insulating the roof. Closed-cell foam ends the cycle mechanically: with the interior surface of the envelope insulated to R-13 or better, the surface the indoor air touches never falls below dew point, so there is nothing to condense on. The foam itself cannot absorb moisture, so there is no wet-blanket failure mode. For warehouses storing paper goods, steel stock, packaged food, or anything else that hates water, condensation control alone has justified more Central Valley foam projects than energy savings ever did.

There is a corrosion dividend, too, that owners only appreciate in year ten. A metal building that sweats every winter is quietly rusting at its fastener points, panel laps, and purlin contacts — the exact locations that determine the building's lifespan. Encapsulating the interior skin in closed-cell foam takes those surfaces off the condensation cycle entirely, which is why insurers and lenders reviewing older steel buildings look kindly on the upgrade. The foam does not just make the building cheaper to run; it makes the building last longer, and in a market where replacing a pre-engineered structure costs multiples of insulating one, that is the quietest return on the whole project.

Offices, Clinics, and the Conditioned-Space Corridor

Not every commercial foam job is a warehouse. Clovis's growth has filled the Herndon corridor around Clovis Community Medical Center with medical office buildings and clinics, and the northeast retail pads keep adding conditioned commercial space. In these buildings foam earns its keep at the roofline and in specific assemblies: sealing and insulating roof decks under mechanical penthouses, quieting and conditioning the envelope of tilt-up shells before tenant improvement, and solving the comfort complaints that follow when a suite's perimeter was value-engineered a decade ago. Conditioned-space work rewards foam's precision — it goes exactly where sprayed, adheres overhead without fasteners, and air-seals as it insulates, which HVAC contractors notice at balancing time. Where the project is the roof itself rather than the interior, the same chemistry works from above as a roofing system; that path — foam as the roof, not under it — is covered in our spray polyurethane foam roofing overview, and many Clovis buildings ultimately do both.

How a Commercial Insulation Project Runs

Commercial foam succeeds or fails on preparation and scheduling discipline, so our process is built around both. It starts with the free assessment: we walk the building, measure, check existing insulation and moisture conditions, and deliver a written bid within 48 hours specifying thickness, R-value, prep, and staging. Before spray day, the areas to be foamed are cleared or masked — we plan around racking, equipment, and operations, and phase large buildings so work continues in occupied zones. Application itself is fast: a crew can foam thousands of square feet of deck per day, with thickness verified as passes build. Ventilation is managed during and after application per SPFA practice, with re-entry timing coordinated so your operation, not the foam, sets the schedule. We close with documented thicknesses for your Title 24 or project file and a walkthrough of the finished envelope. Most retrofits are measured in days, and the building works better the first week than it did the previous decade.

Fire and finish requirements get engineered in, not discovered later. Where code or occupancy requires a thermal or ignition barrier over exposed foam, we include the appropriate coating or covering in the specification from the first bid — it is a known line item, not a surprise, and pretending otherwise is how low bids stay low until permit inspection. Similarly, where a space will be washed down, take physical abuse from forklifts and product, or face food-facility surface requirements, we spec the protective finish that matches the use. A commercial insulation bid that is silent on barriers and finishes is not cheaper; it is incomplete.

If either walk makes the case — and in an unfoamed Valley steel building, one of them almost always does — the assessment will tell you precisely what fixing it costs. How much insulation does a metal building in Clovis actually need?

Two inches of closed-cell foam (about R-13 continuous) is the working floor for most Valley metal buildings — enough to air-seal the skin and stop condensation. Three inches reaches roughly R-19.5 for conditioned or Title 24-driven projects. The right number depends on how the space is used, and the assessment settles it with your actual building, not a rule of thumb.
Will spray foam stop the condensation dripping from my metal roof in winter?

Yes — this is one of the most common reasons Clovis and Sanger building owners call us. Foam insulates the panels so the interior surface stays above dew point during tule-fog weather, and the closed-cell material cannot absorb moisture itself. The purlin drip that soaks inventory every winter ends when the deck is foamed.
Can you spray foam over the old fiberglass in my warehouse?

No — and be wary of anyone who says yes. Compressed, moisture-laden blanket insulation has to come out so foam can bond directly to the panels and fill the purlin cavities properly. We include removal and prep in the written scope so there are no surprises on spray day.
